problem: Front-face headset cameras do inside-out tracking (the cameras look out at the world). 'Outside-in' is the opposite arrangement, where fixed external cameras or base stations look at the headset. The sentence reverses the standard meaning and will confuse students about tracking types.
fix: In a headset, cameras sit on the front face and look outward; this supports inside-out tracking. Outside-in tracking uses external cameras or base stations that look at the headset and controllers.

problem: The tree does not match Section 3. 'Inertial' is noted only 'accel + gyro' although Section 1 puts the magnetometer (heading) in the inertial group, and 'Physiological' is noted only 'gaze' although EMG is the main physiological sensor listed. Touch and flex are labelled 'Environmental' while the chapter's only truly environmental sensor, temperature, is left out.
fix: Use notes such as Inertial: 'accel, gyro, mag'; Environmental: 'temperature, pressure'; Contact/body: 'touch, flex, force'; Physiological: 'EMG, gaze' — so the figure lists the same sensors the text does.

problem: Saying the vector between pupil centre and corneal spot 'gives gaze direction' hides the calibration step. That vector shifts with head position and eye geometry, so the raw vector is not gaze direction until the system is calibrated for that user.
fix: An eye camera finds the pupil centre and the corneal spot; the vector between them is tracked, and after a short per-user calibration this vector is mapped to gaze direction, reported in degrees.
